## Adding a locale

Add an entry to the `locales` block in `astro.config.mjs` and create a matching
directory under `src/content/docs/<locale>/`. Starlight will pick up the new locale
automatically.

## Locale-aware links

Use the generated `Link` component whenever you want to link to another page
**inside** your docs — it automatically resolves the current locale, so a single
source of truth produces the right URL in every language:

```mdx
import Link from '@components/link.astro';

<Link path="guides/getting-started">Read the getting-started guide</Link>
```

Here is the component in action: <Link path="guides/getting-started">back to this page</Link>.

For regular external links, just use ordinary Markdown `[label](url)`.

What this repository documents and how it relates to Discava.

This repository illustrates the **Agentic SDLC** adopted in
[Discava](https://github.com/AlexTo/discava), a serverless, AWS-native Learning
Management System built with AI agents from the start.

It documents the practices, not the product: how work is specified, handed to agents,
verified and shipped.

## The loop at a glance

```d2
direction: right
spec: Spec\n(spec, plan, tasks)
review: Human review
issue: Implementation issue
agent: Agent opens PR
ci: CI checks
merge: Merge to main
deploy: Deploy

spec -> review: spec PR
review -> issue: merged + labelled spec-ready
issue -> agent
agent -> ci
ci -> agent: failure (max 3 retries)
ci -> merge: pass + human review
merge -> issue: next task
merge -> deploy
```

How failing checks send the agent back to fix its work.

When the PR Checks workflow fails on an agent's branch, the **Agent CI Status** workflow posts a
failure commit status that the automation reads, sending the agent back to revise the same pull
request in its original conversation.

- At most **three** fix attempts per PR, tracked with `ci-fix-1` to `ci-fix-3` labels.
- After that the workflow comments and stops (`ci-fix-exhausted`) and a human takes over.
- A passing run posts nothing.

Bounding retries keeps cost predictable and makes sure a stuck agent escalates to a person.
How merged specs become agent-authored pull requests.

1. A merged spec PR labelled `spec-ready` triggers the **Agent Issues** workflow, which opens
   the first implementation issue from `tasks.md`.
2. An implementing agent polls for issues carrying its label and opens a pull request from a
   dedicated branch prefix.
3. The agent's PR ticks the completed tasks in `tasks.md`.
4. When that PR merges, the workflow opens the **next** issue, repeating until the task list is done.

Only the agent's own branches advance the chain; other merged PRs are ignored so the process
cannot loop on its own edits.
How work is defined before an agent touches code.

Each feature starts as a folder under `specs/`, created with [Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit)
skills (`specify`, `clarify`, `plan`, `tasks`, `analyze`). A spec folder contains:

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `spec.md` | What and why: user stories, requirements, acceptance criteria |
| `plan.md` | How: technical approach and design decisions |
| `research.md`, `data-model.md`, `contracts/` | Supporting design detail |
| `tasks.md` | Ordered, checkable implementation tasks |
| `checklists/` | Requirement-quality checklists |

Folders are timestamp-numbered (e.g. `20261115-204447-certificates`).

The spec lands via a normal pull request. A human reviews it, and labelling it `spec-ready`
before merge is the signal to start implementation.
The few ideas the whole workflow is built from.

Everything in this workflow follows from one move: **take the developer out of the loop and put
them at its two ends.** Humans decide *what* to build and *whether it is good*. Agents do
everything in between, through the normal GitHub process.

## 1. The spec is the source of truth

A feature starts as `spec.md`, `plan.md` and `tasks.md`, reviewed like code. The agent generates
the code from them. To change behaviour you change the spec and regenerate; you don't patch the
code by hand and let the spec go stale.

## 2. Every step leaves an artifact

Intent lives in the spec, scope in the issue, history in the pull request. Nothing lives in a chat
window or someone's head, so a new teammate or a new agent can pick up where the last one stopped.

## 3. Small, scoped units of work

A spec splits into phases. Each phase is one issue and one pull request, with a task range the
agent must not leave. Small PRs are cheap to review and cheap to throw away.

## 4. Automated gates give the feedback, not you

Lint, typecheck, unit tests, invariants, e2e tests, concurrency tests, screenshots and an agent
reviewer all run on every PR. A red result goes straight back to the agent that wrote the change.
Nobody pastes an error message.

## 5. Bounded autonomy

The agent can't merge, can't edit workflows, can't touch credentials and can't weaken a test to get
green. Each fix-up loop is capped at three attempts; then it stops and asks a human.

## 6. Humans keep the two decisions that matter

1. **Approve the spec.** Merging the spec PR (labelled `spec-ready`) is the go signal.
2. **Approve the result.** A person does the final review and merges each PR.

## 7. Docs are part of the change, not an afterthought

A feature isn't done until the docs describe it. Documentation is a task in `tasks.md`, done by the
agent in the same chain of PRs, and checked by the same gates.

The feature every tutorial step builds, and why it was chosen.

The tutorial follows one feature from idea to merged code: **tags on notes**.

> A user can add up to five tags to a note, and filter the note list by tag.

It is small enough to finish in a few PRs, and it touches every layer of the example notes app, so
each stage of the workflow has something real to do.

| Layer | What changes | Which gate catches mistakes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `notes-table` | `tags` attribute on the `note` entity | Unit tests |
| `notes-api` | `tags` on create and update, `tag` filter on list | Unit tests, typecheck |
| `notes-website` | Tag input on the note form, tag chips, tag filter | Screenshots, e2e |
| Business rule | Max five tags, no duplicates, case-insensitive | Invariants, unit tests |
| Concurrency | Two tabs adding tags at once must not lose either | Concurrency test |
| `docs/` | The notes app page describes tags | Agent review, human review |

## The phases

The spec is split into three phases, so three issues and three PRs:

1. **Data and API.** Entity, procedures, validation rules, unit tests.
2. **Website.** Tag input, chips, filter, e2e scenario with screenshots, invariant and concurrency tests.
3. **Docs.** Update the docs to describe tags.

<Aside type="note">
The phases in this case are an example. Your own specs will split differently. The rule is only that
each phase is one reviewable PR that leaves `main` working.
</Aside>

**You are here:** agent, unattended. **Output:** a pull request for phase 1 on an `openhands/...` branch.

Within about 15 minutes OpenHands polls for issues labelled `openhands` and picks up the issue.
You do nothing. This is what it does, and what you can check on the PR afterwards.

## What the agent does

1. Reads `CLAUDE.md`, the constitution, and the spec folder.
2. Writes the tests for the phase first: the tag rules from the spec, as unit tests.
3. Implements until they pass, ticking each task in `tasks.md` in the same commit that completes it.
4. Runs lint, typecheck, build and unit tests on what it changed, once, not in watch mode.
5. Opens a PR titled as a Conventional Commit, for example
   `feat(notes): add tags to notes in the data and API layers`, with `Refs #<parent>` in the body.
6. Lists the **(human)** tasks it skipped.

## What it is told not to do

The issue template spells the limits out, and the workflows enforce the important ones:

- Never work outside the task range.
- Never weaken a test to make it pass.
- Never edit `.github/workflows/`, never merge, never touch credentials.
- If it's blocked, comment on the issue and stop. It does not guess.

## What you check

Open the PR and read it from the top:

- Does the title and body tell you what changed and which tasks are done?
- Are the tests testing the *spec's* rules, or the implementation's quirks?
- Is `tasks.md` ticked for exactly this phase and no more?

<Aside type="tip">
You don't have to review yet. CI and the agent reviewer go first, and the PR only reaches you once
they are happy. See the next step.
</Aside>

import { Steps, Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**You are here:** human gate #1. **Output:** a merged spec PR and the first implementation issue.

<Steps>

1. Open the spec PR.

   ```bash
   git add specs/ && git commit -m "docs(specs): add note tags spec"
   git push -u origin spec/note-tags
   gh pr create --fill
   ```

2. Review it as you would code. Read `spec.md` first, then `plan.md`, then skim `tasks.md`.
   Ask yourself:

   - Does the spec say what you actually want?
   - Is each phase small enough to review in one sitting?
   - Is anything in the plan something you would reject in a code review?

   Comment on the PR to change anything. The agent reads comments too, so you can ask it to revise.

3. Label the PR `spec-ready`, then merge.

   ```bash
   gh pr edit --add-label spec-ready
   gh pr merge --squash
   ```

</Steps>

## What happens next, with no one touching anything

The **Agent Issues** workflow sees a merged PR carrying `spec-ready`. It reads `tasks.md`, takes
the first unfinished phase and opens an issue from the
[implementation template](https://github.com/AlexTo/agentic-sdlc/blob/main/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/implement-phase.md):
spec folder, task range `T001` to `T003`, and the rules the agent must follow. It adds the
`openhands` label, which is the go signal.

<Aside type="note">
Forgot the label? Add `spec-ready` to the already merged PR, or run the workflow by hand with the
spec folder name. Nothing else is needed.
</Aside>

Your attention is now free until there is something to review. Next: [Agent implements](../agent-implements/).
Automated gates and bounded fix-up loops, with no human in between.

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**You are here:** automation, unattended. **Output:** a green PR with an approving agent review.

Every push to the agent's PR runs the gates. Failures go back to the agent, never to you.

## The gates

| Gate | What it catches in the tags case |
| --- | --- |
| Lint, typecheck, build | An API type that no longer matches the entity |
| Unit tests | A sixth tag accepted, or `Work` and `work` stored as two tags |
| Invariants | Any note in the table with more than five tags, after every e2e test |
| E2E tests | The tag input doesn't save, or the filter shows the wrong notes |
| Concurrency test | Two simultaneous adds overwrite each other and one tag is lost |
| Screenshots | The new UI was never looked at: the `UI Screenshots` check fails |
| Tasks format check | A malformed `tasks.md` that would stall the chain |

## When a gate fails

1. The **Agent CI Status** workflow posts a failing commit status that the agent already watches.
2. The agent revises the *same* PR in its original conversation, using the failure output.
3. CI runs again.

An example: the concurrency test fails because adding a tag reads the note, appends in memory and
writes it back, so two requests race. The agent changes it to an atomic append with a condition on
the count, and the test goes green. You never saw it.

## Agent review

Once CI is green, a second OpenHands agent reviews the PR as a person would: correctness, missed
edge cases, rules from the spec that no test covers. It either approves, or requests changes, which
sends the implementing agent back the same way a red CI does.

## The cap

Each loop is limited to **three** attempts, tracked with `ci-fix-1` to `ci-fix-3` labels. After
the third, the workflow comments, adds `ci-fix-exhausted` and stops.

<Aside type="caution">
`ci-fix-exhausted` is the one time you are pulled in early. Read the last failure, then either
comment with guidance, fix it yourself, or go back to the spec: repeated failure often means the
spec was ambiguous. Fixing the spec and regenerating beats patching the code.
</Aside>

**You are here:** human gate #2. **Output:** phase 1 merged, phase 2's issue open.

The PR reaches you green and approved by the agent reviewer. Your job is to judge the outcome,

<Steps>

1. Read the PR description and the **E2E screenshots** comment. For the website phase, this is

2. Check the **(human)** tasks the agent listed and do them.

3. Approve and merge, or comment to request changes. A "changes requested" sends the agent back,

   ```bash

   ```

## What merging does

The **Agent Issues** workflow sees a merged PR on an `openhands/` branch, reads the ticked
`tasks.md`, and opens the issue for the next phase. Phase 2 (the website) now runs exactly as
phase 1 did: tests first, PR, gates, fix-ups, review.

Only the agent's own branches advance the chain. A PR you merge by hand is ignored, so the process
can't loop on its own edits.

```text
spec PR merged ─► issue 1 ─► PR 1 merged ─► issue 2 ─► PR 2 merged ─► issue 3 ─► PR 3 merged ─► done
   (you)                       (you)                      (you)                      (you)
```

Between each of your clicks, nothing needs you. When the last phase merges, no further issue opens
and the feature is complete.

Derive the technical plan and an ordered task list, then check them against the spec.

import { Steps, Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**You are here:** human + agent. **Output:** `plan.md`, `data-model.md`, `contracts/` and `tasks.md`.

<Steps>

1. Generate the plan.

   ```text
   /speckit-plan
   ```

   The plan reads the spec and the project constitution (`.specify/memory/constitution.md`) and
   decides *how*: add `tags` to the ElectroDB entity, extend the tRPC input schemas, add a
   `tag` filter to `notes.list`.

2. Generate the tasks.

   ```text
   /speckit-tasks
   ```

   `tasks.md` is ordered, checkable and grouped by phase. For the docs and review steps to work,
   the format matters: every task has an ID, and phases are separate headings.

   ```markdown
   ## Phase 1: Data and API
   - [ ] T001 Add `tags` to the note entity in packages/notes-table/src/entities/note.ts
   - [ ] T002 [P] Unit tests for tag rules (max five, unique, case-insensitive)
   - [ ] T003 Extend create and update procedures in packages/notes-api/src/procedures/notes.ts

   ## Phase 2: Website
   - [ ] T004 Tag input on the note form
   - [ ] T005 Tag filter on the list page
   - [ ] T006 e2e scenario with screenshots, invariant and concurrency tests

   ## Phase 3: Docs
   - [ ] T007 Describe tags on the notes app page in docs/
   - [ ] T008 **(human)** Confirm the screenshots match the docs wording
   ```

3. Cross-check everything before any code exists.

   ```text
   /speckit-analyze
   ```

   It reports requirements with no task, tasks with no requirement, and contradictions between
   the three files. Fix them now; it costs a sentence. After implementation it costs a PR.

</Steps>

<Aside type="caution">
A malformed `tasks.md` would stall the pipeline silently, so a PR check validates its format.
You will see that check run in the next step.
</Aside>

Tasks marked **(human)** are skipped by the agent and listed in its PR description for you.

**You are here:** agent, then human gate #2 again. **Output:** the docs describe tags.

Phase 3 is not different in kind from the others. The docs are code (this site is MDX in
`docs/`), so the same chain handles them.

## What the agent does

Given the issue for tasks `T007` to `T008`, the agent:

1. Reads the spec and the merged code from phases 1 and 2. The spec says what the feature is for;
   the code says what it does.
2. Updates the notes app page: the `tags` attribute, the new API input and filter, and the rules
   (five tags, unique, case-insensitive), phrased exactly as the spec states them.
3. Reuses the screenshots from the e2e scenario instead of inventing new ones, so the docs show
   what the app really does.
4. Builds the docs site, so a broken link or malformed MDX fails the PR like any other build error.

## What you check

- Does every rule on the page match a requirement in `spec.md`?
- If the docs and the spec disagree, **the spec wins.** Change the spec, not the docs by hand.
- Is anything documented that the code doesn't do?

## Why it's in the chain

Docs written after the fact, by a different person, from memory, drift. Docs generated from the
spec and the merged code, in the same workflow, and reviewed with the same gates, don't. The agent
reviewer is also a cheap second reader: it flags a docs claim that no test or code backs up.

<Aside type="tip">
When you change behaviour later, start at the spec again. Update it, regenerate the plan and
tasks, and the docs phase comes round with the rest.
</Aside>

## Done

Merge the docs PR. With no tasks left, no new issue opens, and the feature has gone from one
sentence to merged code and docs, with your hands on exactly two decisions per PR: approving the
spec, and approving the result.

Turn the idea into spec.md with Speckit, and have the agent challenge it.

import { Steps, Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**You are here:** human + agent. **Output:** `specs/<timestamp>-note-tags/spec.md`.

The spec says *what* and *why*, never *how*. It is the most important thing you write.

<Steps>

1. Start from a branch.

   ```bash
   git switch -c spec/note-tags
   ```

2. Describe the feature to Speckit.

   ```text
   /speckit-specify Users can add up to five tags to a note and filter the note list by tag.
   Tags are case-insensitive and unique per note.
   ```

   Speckit creates `specs/<timestamp>-note-tags/spec.md` with user stories, functional
   requirements and acceptance criteria.

3. Let the agent find the gaps.

   ```text
   /speckit-clarify
   ```

   It asks up to five targeted questions and writes your answers back into the spec. For this
   feature, expect questions such as:

   - What happens when a sixth tag is added: reject, or drop the oldest?
   - Is `Work` the same tag as `work`? (The spec says yes: lowercase on save.)
   - Is there a maximum tag length?

</Steps>

## What good looks like

- Each user story can be tested on its own, with acceptance scenarios written as Given/When/Then.
- Every rule is stated as a requirement, for example *"A note MUST NOT have more than five tags."*
  Those rules become the invariants and tests later.
- No technology appears in the spec. No DynamoDB, no tRPC.

<Aside type="tip">
Answer the clarification questions yourself instead of letting the agent guess. Each answer you
give is one fewer wrong assumption in the code.
</Aside>
